kiddushin-33a-15-15.note: Ravina was sitting with Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man passed by with his head uncovered, and Ravina called him rude for not honoring a rabbi. Rabbi Yirmeya suggested he might be from Mata Mehasya, where there are many rabbis, so people there are less careful to show that kind of honor.

kiddushin-39a-10-11.note: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan, traveling outside the Land of Israel, saw a man planting mixed kinds of seeds. One suggested ostracizing him, but the other said he did not understand the laws. Then they saw a man planting wheat and barley among grapevines, and again the same exchange followed. The second explained that, following Rabbi Yoshiya, a person is not liable by Torah law unless he sows wheat, barley and a grape seed in a single motion, so this man should not be ostracized.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on mixing certain kinds of plants, such as sowing different seeds together.
To formally shun someone as a punishment.

kiddushin-39b-13-13.note: Some say a man saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, who had been executed by the government, lying in the street and dragged by a pig (the text says 'something else', a polite way of saying this). He asked whether a mouth that produced pearls should lap up dirt. The text says that for this reason he went out and sinned.

people.name: Hutzpit the disseminator
people.about: a sage executed by the government

terms.meaning: A person who stood beside a teacher and repeated his words aloud to the crowd.

kiddushin-39b-15-15.note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He used a spoken formula to cover himself in boils so she would be repelled, but she used magic to heal him, so he fled and hid overnight in a bathhouse so haunted that two people entering together were harmed even by day. Next morning he told the Sages that angels in the form of two soldiers had guarded him all night. The Sages answered that a miracle like this happens to someone who was tempted toward forbidden intercourse and resisted, and they cited a verse about Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: named in the closing verse as an example of someone saved from such temptation

terms.meaning: a noblewoman, a woman of high social standing.
a soldier of the emperor, an imperial guard.

kiddushin-40a-1-1.note: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok. He said he was too weak and needed food, and she offered non-kosher food. He said the one who commits this act would eat such food too, and when she lit the oven to roast it, he climbed into the oven. He explained that the one who does this act falls into the fires of Gehenna (hell). She replied that had she known how serious it was to him, she would not have caused him such distress, and the passage ends there, with him spared.

terms.meaning: the place of fiery punishment after death, roughly like hell.

kiddushin-40a-2-2.note: Rav Kahana sold palm-leaf baskets to women, and a noblewoman tried to seduce him. He said he would first go adorn himself, climbed to the roof, and fell off. Elijah the prophet caught him and complained that saving him meant traveling four hundred parasangs. Rav Kahana answered that poverty, which forced him into a trade that brought him near women, was the cause, and Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars so he would not have to keep selling.

people.name: Elijah the prophet
people.about: the biblical prophet, who in Jewish tradition appears to rescue people

terms.meaning: an ancient Persian unit of distance, a few miles.
a coin of the period.

kiddushin-45b-3-3.note: A couple wanted to marry off their minor daughter. The father wanted her to marry his relative and the mother wanted her to marry hers; the mother pressured him until he agreed to her relative. While they were eating the festive meal before the betrothal, the father's relative came up to the roof and betrothed the girl to himself. The passage ends with this act, with no ruling stated in the text.

terms.meaning: the first stage of Jewish marriage, a formal act that binds a couple legally before they live together.

kiddushin-50a-9-9.note: A man sold his property after telling the buyer he planned to move to the Land of Israel. He went but could not settle there, came back to Babylonia, and tried to cancel the sale. Rava ruled that people go to Israel intending to settle, so since he could not, he can cancel the sale. A second version of the tradition says Rava ruled the opposite: he intended to go and did go, so the sale stands.

terms.meaning: the Land of Israel.

kiddushin-50a-10-10.note: A similar case: a man sold his property intending to move to the Land of Israel but never went. Rav Ashi ruled the sale stands, since he could have gone had he wanted and the matter was up to him. A second version words this as a question. The Gemara says the two versions differ only if something outside his control stopped him: the first version still upholds the sale, the second implies it would be cancelled.

terms.meaning: the Talmud's discussion and analysis that builds on the Mishnah.

kiddushin-52b-12-14.note: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students to keep Meir's students out of the study hall, calling them troublemakers who came to overwhelm him with legal questions rather than to learn. Sumakhos pushed in and quoted Meir's ruling that a priest cannot betroth a woman using his share of the Temple offerings. Yehuda got angry and said the case is irrelevant since a woman could not be in that part of the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Yosei spoke up, fearing people would say Meir died, Yehuda got angry, and Yosei stayed silent. He argued the ruling is relevant: a father or a woman's agent could accept the betrothal there, and a woman might push her way in.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: a sage who had died; his students are the subject

terms.meaning: to legally begin a marriage by giving the woman something of value.
a teaching from the sages of the Mishnah era that is not in the Mishnah itself.

kiddushin-57a-0-1.note: A teaching says Shimon HaAmasoni (some say Nehemya HaAmasoni) used to interpret every appearance of the small word 'et' in the Torah to derive extra laws. When he reached 'You shall fear the Lord your God', he stopped, since nothing could be added to the fear of God. His students asked what would become of all his earlier interpretations, and he said that just as he was rewarded for interpreting, he was rewarded for stopping. Later Rabbi Akiva taught that here 'et' includes Torah scholars, meaning they are to be feared too.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: some say it was Nehemya HaAmasoni

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: later explained the word 'et' in this verse

terms.meaning: a small Hebrew word marking the object of a sentence, which some sages read as hinting at an additional law.
a teaching from the sages of the Mishnah era that is not in the Mishnah itself.

kiddushin-59a-5-7.note: Rav Giddel was in the middle of buying a plot of land when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel's complaint passed through Rabbi Zeira to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who asked Rabbi Abba whether it is wrong to snatch a poor man's found loaf; Abba said the taker is wicked. Abba said he had not known of Giddel's attempt but would not sell the land, his first purchase, though he would give it as a gift. Giddel would not take a gift, and Abba then would not take the land either, so it was called the land of the Sages.

terms.meaning: one of the three holidays when Jews traditionally traveled to the Temple, here a time when scholars gathered.

kiddushin-66a-5-5.note: Abaye cites a case to support a point. A blind man who reviewed Mishnah with Mar Shmuel was late, so Shmuel sent a messenger to help him. The messenger missed him, went to his house, and returned saying he had seen the man's wife commit adultery. The blind man asked whether he must act on this. Mar Shmuel ruled that if he trusts the messenger he should divorce her, and if not he should not.

terms.meaning: the paragraphs of the Mishnah, the early code of Jewish law that students memorized and reviewed.

kiddushin-66a-7-11.note: King Yannai conquered sixty cities and held a feast with the Sages. A scoffer, Elazar ben Po'ira, told him the Sages secretly resented him and suggested making them stand before his High Priest frontplate. The elder Yehuda ben Gedidya said Yannai should leave the priesthood to Aaron's descendants, citing a rumor that his mother had been captured, which could disqualify him. The rumor was never proven, and the Sages were expelled. Elazar urged him to kill them; Yannai asked what would become of the Torah, and Elazar said it could be studied from a scroll. The Sages were killed, and the world lacked Torah until Shimon ben Shatah restored it.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: a king who was also High Priest, of the priestly Hasmonean family

people.name: Elazar ben Po'ira
people.about: a scoffer present at the feast

terms.meaning: a priest's child disqualified from the priesthood because of a forbidden marriage in the family line.
the traditional teachings passed down by the Sages alongside the written text.

kiddushin-70a-11-16.note: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda in a butcher shop in Pumbedita, so Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and declared him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to the court of Rav Nahman. Rav Huna advised that he need not go, but should for the honor of the Exilarch's house. In Neharde'a, Rav Yehuda corrected Rav Nahman's word choices and refused to let his daughter serve or his wife be greeted, citing Shmuel's rulings. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, so the outcome of the dispute is not shown.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: a judge in Neharde'a, son-in-law of the Exilarch

terms.meaning: formally cut off from the community as a penalty.
the head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

kiddushin-70b-1-8.note: Rav Nahman denied sending the summons, but Rav Yehuda showed it, and Nahman insisted on hearing the case so no one could say the Sages go easy on each other. Rav Yehuda justified excommunicating the man and calling him a slave, since he called others slaves, which Shmuel said shows one's own flawed lineage. When the man claimed Hasmonean royal descent, Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel that anyone saying so is a slave. Nahman objected that Yehuda was personally involved, so Rav Mattana confirmed Shmuel's statement. That day marriages in Neharde'a were annulled, and when a mob chased Rav Yehuda, he threatened to reveal Shmuel's remark about the dove's house and raven's house, and they dropped their stones.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: quoted for his ruling about the Hasmoneans

terms.meaning: the priestly royal family that ruled Judea after the Maccabee revolt.
formally cut off from the community as a penalty.

kiddushin-71a-4-5.note: In Rabbi Pinehas's time, some wanted to portray Babylonian family lineage as doubtful compared to that of the Land of Israel. He told his servants to carry him off on a stretcher after he spoke twice in the study hall. He first said bird slaughter is not required by Torah law, and while they debated it, he said the lineage of every land is doubtful compared to Israel's, and Israel's compared to Babylonia's. His servants ran off with him and the scholars could not catch him. They then checked families' lineage but stopped when they reached powerful families, since accusing them was dangerous.

terms.meaning: a family's ancestry, which affects whom its members may marry.

kiddushin-71b-2-2.note: Ze'eiri, a Babylonian sage, kept avoiding Rabbi Yohanan of the Land of Israel because Yohanan kept asking him to marry his daughter. One day they came to a large puddle, and Ze'eiri lifted Yohanan onto his shoulders and carried him across. Yohanan then asked how Ze'eiri could honor his Torah yet treat his daughters as unfit, and why he would not marry her. The passage ends with the question, and no answer is given.

kiddushin-71b-4-8.note: Ulla visited Pumbedita and saw that Rav Yehuda's grown son Rav Yitzhak was unmarried. Rav Yehuda said he worried about finding a woman of sound lineage. Ulla replied that none of us can be sure of our own ancestry, since we may descend from women assaulted during wars or from people the prophet Amos condemned, and Rabbi Abbahu says some descend from wife-swapping groups, which produces mamzerim. When Rav Yehuda asked how to tell, Ulla said to follow the silence. In the Land of Israel, when two people quarrel, the one who goes silent first is considered to be of finer lineage.

terms.meaning: a person born from certain forbidden unions, who is restricted in whom they may marry.

kiddushin-73a-5-5.note: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and everyone pelted him with their etrogim because the many converts felt insulted. Rava said he should have been more careful in a place with many converts. Rava first taught there that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. He then taught the mamzeret ruling, and they said he had lost the honor of his first sermon. Rava answered that he had done what was good for them: a convert may marry from pure lineage or from a mamzeret, as he wishes.

terms.meaning: a woman born from certain forbidden unions, who is restricted in whom she may marry.
a citron, the fruit used on the holiday of Sukkot.

kiddushin-76b-9-10.note: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host, a convert's son, and Rav Beivai both wanted the city's official position, so they went to Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef cited a verse about appointing a king 'from among your brothers' to show that a convert cannot hold official positions. Rav Adda asked about someone whose mother is born Jewish, and Rav Yosef said the verse allows it. He ruled that Rav Beivai, a great Torah scholar, oversee religious matters and the host oversee the city's other matters. Abaye's moral was to host someone like Rav Adda bar Ahava, whose pleading won his host his post.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: his host's advocate in this story

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: described as a great man in Torah learning

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: the sage who decided the dispute

people.name: Abaye
people.about: gave the moral of the story

terms.meaning: someone not born Jewish who joined the Jewish people.

kiddushin-80a-4-4.note: A woman came to Jerusalem with a child riding on her shoulders, as a mother would, and raised him. He later had intercourse with her, and the court stoned them for the prohibition on a mother and son. The text says this was not because he was definitely her son, since there was no testimony of that, but because he clung to her and so had the presumed status of her son.

terms.meaning: treating a person as having a certain status because of how things appear, even without proof.

kiddushin-80b-11-11.note: The Rabbis are described as concerned about sin even in times of deep grief. As an example, a woman visiting her husband's grave had intercourse with a man guarding the body of someone executed by the king. Meanwhile that body was taken, and she suggested digging up her husband so the guard could claim he had done his job. The point is that even in mourning a person can give in to temptation.

terms.meaning: to dig up a buried body.

kiddushin-81a-10-11.note: Captive women who had been redeemed were lodged in the upper room of Rav Amram the Pious's house, and the ladder was removed to keep men from them. One woman was so beautiful that it seemed a light shone from the doorway, and Rav Amram lifted a ladder that ten men could not lift and began to climb. Halfway up, he braced himself and shouted that his house was on fire. The Sages came and said he had embarrassed them, and he replied that it was better to be shamed in this world than before them in the World-to-Come. He then made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire and said that although it was fire and he was flesh, he had beaten it.

terms.meaning: the inner urge toward sin that Jewish tradition says every person struggles with.
the afterlife, where a person's deeds are judged.

kiddushin-81a-12-12.note: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners by saying it is easy to resist temptation. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river, and Meir crossed a rope bridge toward her. Halfway across, the evil inclination left him and said that if it were not proclaimed in heaven to take care of Rabbi Meir and his Torah, it would have made his blood worth two small coins. The passage ends there, with Meir spared and the lesson that no one is above temptation.

terms.meaning: in rabbinic tradition, the force that tempts people to sin.
a very small coin.

kiddushin-81a-13-13.note: Like Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Akiva used to ridicule people who sin. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree, and Akiva grabbed the tree and began to climb. Halfway up, the evil inclination left him and said that if it were not proclaimed in heaven to take care of Rabbi Akiva and his Torah, it would have made his blood worth two small coins. The lesson, as in the previous story, is that even great scholars are not immune to temptation.

terms.meaning: the inner urge toward sin that Jewish tradition says every person struggles with.
a very small coin.

kiddushin-81a-14-14.note: Peleimu used to say every day, 'An arrow in the eye of Satan.' On the eve of Yom Kippur, Satan came to his door as a poor man asking for food and kept asking to be let in until he sat at Peleimu's table, where he behaved disgustingly and spat into a cup. When people scolded him, he pretended to die, and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man, so Peleimu fled and hid in the bathroom. Satan followed him, revealed himself, and asked why Peleimu kept provoking him. He told Peleimu to say instead, 'Let the Merciful One rebuke the Satan.'

terms.meaning: in rabbinic tradition, the force that tempts people to sin.
the Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.
a common Aramaic way of referring to God.

kiddushin-81b-1-3.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi would pray each day to be saved from the evil inclination. His wife, who knew he had stayed away from her for years, wondered why he needed to pray that. One day she dressed up, walked past him in the garden, and said she was Haruta, a well-known prostitute. He propositioned her, climbed a tree for a pomegranate as her price, and they had intercourse. At home he sat in the burning oven in guilt, and when she told him it was her, he did not believe her until she gave him proofs. He said he had still intended to sin, fasted for the rest of his life over it, and died in his misery.

people.name: Haruta
people.about: the name his wife gave when posing as a prostitute

terms.meaning: the inner urge toward sin that Jewish tradition says every person struggles with.

kiddushin-81b-14-14.note: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and put his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether she might already be betrothed. Rav Aha replied that if so Rav Hisda had broken Rav's ruling against betrothing a minor daughter. Rav Hisda answered that Rav Aha had broken Shmuel's rule against making use of a woman. Rav Aha answered with another statement of Shmuel that such actions are permitted for the sake of Heaven, meaning out of family affection without any improper element.

terms.meaning: to begin a marriage legally; a girl who has been betrothed is treated as another man's wife.
done with a pure, proper motive.
